## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Run R code in the browser and change it.
2. Use R as a calculator, including the order of operations.
3. Call a function such as `sqrt()` or `round()`.
4. Read an error message and fix the code.
5. Find help on any function with `?`.

## What is R?

R is a free programming language for working with data. You write instructions, called **code**, and R carries them out. Analysts use R to clean data, run statistics, draw charts and write reports.

If you use Excel, think of R as a formula bar with no spreadsheet attached. You type `=SUM(A1:A10)` in Excel. In R you type `sum(x)`. The difference is that R keeps every step as text, so you can rerun the whole analysis tomorrow with new data.

## Your first code

The box below is a live R session. Click **Run Code**.

::: {.callout-note}
The first run takes a few seconds while R loads in your browser. After that, code runs straight away.
:::

```{webr}
1 + 1
```

R printed `[1] 2`. The `2` is the answer. The `[1]` means "this is the first value of the result". You will see why that is useful on Day 3.

Now change the code to `10 * 7` and run it again. You cannot break anything: refresh the page to start over.

## R as a calculator

R uses the same symbols as a calculator:

| Symbol | Meaning | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `+` | add | `5 + 3` | 8 |
| `-` | subtract | `5 - 3` | 2 |
| `*` | multiply | `5 * 3` | 15 |
| `/` | divide | `5 / 2` | 2.5 |
| `^` | power | `5 ^ 2` | 25 |
| `%%` | remainder | `5 %% 2` | 1 |

R follows the normal order of operations: brackets first, then powers, then multiplying and dividing, then adding and subtracting.

```{webr}
2 + 3 * 4     # multiplication first: 2 + 12
(2 + 3) * 4   # brackets first: 5 * 4
```

Everything after `#` is a **comment**. R ignores it. Use comments to explain your code to other people and to your future self.

## Calling functions

A **function** is a named command that does a job. You write its name, then brackets, and put the input inside the brackets.

```{webr}
sqrt(81)          # square root
round(3.14159, 2) # round to 2 decimal places
abs(-12)          # absolute value
```

`round()` takes two inputs, separated by a comma: the number and the number of decimal places. The inputs are called **arguments**. You will learn more about them on Day 5.

## Text in R

Text goes inside quotation marks. R calls text a **string**.

```{webr}
"Hello, R"
toupper("hello, r")
nchar("Kampala")
```

`nchar()` counts the characters in a string.

## Reading error messages

Errors are normal. Professional programmers see them all day. The message tells you what went wrong. Run this code:

```{webr}
sqrt("nine") # Error expected: read the message below
```

R says `non-numeric argument to mathematical function`. In plain English: "`sqrt()` needs a number, but you gave it text". Fix it by replacing `"nine"` with `9`.

Here are three errors you will meet often:

- `Error: object 'x' not found`: you used a name that R does not know. Check the spelling.
- `Error: unexpected ')'`: a bracket is missing or extra.
- `could not find function "squrt"`: the function name is misspelt.

## Getting help

Every function has a help page. In RStudio, type `?` and the function name in the Console:

```r
?round
```

Help pages can look dense at first. Read the **Usage** section (how to call the function), the **Arguments** section (what each input means) and the **Examples** at the bottom.

::: {.callout-note}
## In this browser
Help pages do not open in the browser version of R. Use `args()` to see a function's arguments, or search for "R round function" online. The full help pages are also at [rdocumentation.org](https://www.rdocumentation.org).
:::

```{webr}
args(round)
```

## Exercises

Each exercise checks your answer when you click **Run Code**. Replace the `______` blanks with your code.

### Exercise 1: Order of operations

A shop sells 3 notebooks at 2,500 shillings each and 2 pens at 800 shillings each. Write one line of code that calculates the total cost.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1_total
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex1_total"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Multiply each price by the quantity, then add the two results: `3 * 2500 + ______`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex1_total"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
3 * 2500 + 2 * 800
```
Multiplication happens before addition, so no brackets are needed. The total is 9,100 shillings.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1_total
#| check: true
if (!is.numeric(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Your answer should be a number. Did you put it in quotes?")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 9100))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 9,100 shillings.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, (3 * 2500 + 2) * 800))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Check your brackets. Multiply each item by its own price.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Work out notebooks and pens separately, then add them.")
}
```

### Exercise 2: Use a function

Round the number `2 / 3` to 3 decimal places.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1_round
round(______, ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex1_round"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The first argument is the number to round. The second is how many decimal places you want.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex1_round"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
round(2 / 3, 3)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1_round
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 0.667))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 0.667.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, round(2 / 3)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You rounded to 0 decimal places. Add the number of digits as the second argument.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. You should get 0.667.")
}
```

### Exercise 3: Fix the error

This code should give the square root of 144, but it has an error. Run it, read the message, then fix it.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1_fix
squrt(144)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex1_fix"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The error says `could not find function`. Check the spelling of the function name against the examples above.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex1_fix"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
sqrt(144)
```
The function is called `sqrt`, short for "square root".
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1_fix
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 12))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Fixed. The square root of 144 is 12.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The answer should be 12. Check the function name.")
}
```

### Exercise 4: Count characters

How many characters are in the word `"Mbarara"`? Use a function to find out.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1_nchar
______("Mbarara")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex1_nchar"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Look at the "Text in R" section. One function counts characters.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex1_nchar"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
nchar("Mbarara")
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1_nchar
#| check: true
if (identical(as.integer(.result), 7L)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 7 characters.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Use nchar().")
}
```

## Run R on your own computer

You can finish Days 1 to 14 in the browser. When you want to work on your own data, follow the [setup guide](../setup.qmd) to install R and RStudio. Everything you learnt today works the same way in the RStudio **Console**.

## Common mistakes

- **Typing the `[1]`.** It is part of R's output, not part of the code.
- **Forgetting the closing bracket.** In RStudio, a `+` at the start of the line means R is waiting for you to finish. Type the missing `)` or press Esc.
- **Using curly quotes.** Code copied from a word processor may have “curly” quotes. R needs straight quotes: `"` or `'`.
- **Capital letters.** R is case-sensitive. `Sqrt(9)` fails. `sqrt(9)` works.

## Summary

- R carries out code and prints the result. `[1]` marks the first value.
- R follows the normal order of operations. Use brackets to make the order clear.
- A function has a name and brackets: `round(3.14159, 2)`. Its inputs are arguments.
- Text goes inside quotes.
- Error messages tell you what is wrong. Read them, then fix the code.
- `?function_name` opens the help page.

**Tomorrow:** you will save values with names, so you can reuse them.
